entry: Computer software released under a license permitting anyone to use, study, modify, and distribute it for any purpose. Such rights are typically granted through open licenses or, more rarely, by dedication to the [[Public domain|public domain]]. Development can rely on open collaboration, a decentralized model of production. Major examples include the [[Linux]] kernel, the [[Firefox]] web browser and [[Bitcoin]]. A 2022 estimate suggests that between 80 and 96 percent of code in software on the market, including proprietary software, is of open-source origin. The term was formalized in 1998 with the founding of the Open Source Initiative.

Art form of Western theatre in which music is fundamental and dramatic roles are taken by singers. Works are typically collaborations between a composer and a librettist, performed with an orchestra in an opera house. Opera originated in Italy at the end of the 16th century, especially through [[Claudio Monteverdi]]'s *L'Orfeo*, and soon spread through Europe. Italian opera dominated most of Europe in the 18th century, except France. [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]] is the most renowned figure of late 18th-century opera. The mid-to-late 19th century was a golden age led by [[Giuseppe Verdi]] in Italy and [[Richard Wagner]] in Germany. The 20th century brought experiments with modern styles, including atonality, neoclassicism, and minimalism, while recordings made singers such as [[Enrico Caruso]] and [[Maria Callas]] known to much wider audiences.

System software that manages [[Computer hardware|computer hardware]] and software resources and provides common services for computer programs. It acts as an intermediary between programs and hardware, allocating processor time and memory, isolating applications from one another, and providing an interface that abstracts hardware access. Operating systems run on devices from cellular phones to web servers and [[Supercomputer|supercomputers]]. As of November 2025, [[Android (operating system)|Android]] had the largest market share, at 38%, followed by [[Microsoft Windows]] at 33%, [[IOS|iOS]] and iPadOS at 15%, [[MacOS|macOS]] at 4%, and [[Linux]] at 1%. Linux distributions dominate the server and supercomputing sectors. Specialized types include embedded and real-time systems, and security-focused systems also exist.

Axis invasion of the [[Soviet Union]] during [[World War II]], launched by [[Nazi Germany]] and several European allies on June 22, 1941. More than 3.8 million Axis troops invaded along a 2,900-kilometer (1,800 mi) front, making it the largest and costliest military offensive in human history. The Axis captured five million Soviet [[Red Army]] troops, and 3.3 million prisoners of war were deliberately starved to death or otherwise killed, as well as millions of civilians. Mass shootings and gassing operations murdered over a million Soviet Jews as part of the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. Its failure reversed the fortunes of Nazi Germany.

Indian military operation, June 1–10, 1984, to remove militants led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale from the [[Golden Temple]], the holiest site of [[Sikhism]], in [[Amritsar]]. Heavy weapons, including [[Tank|tanks]], [[Helicopter|helicopters]], and [[Artillery|artillery]], were used after an initial assault with light weapons failed. Many civilians were subject to extrajudicial killings by the military. Sikhs worldwide criticized the attack. Five months later, Prime Minister [[Indira Gandhi]] was assassinated by two Sikh bodyguards, and anti-Sikh riots followed. The operation has been described as disastrous for the Indian military and state, and it spawned an insurgency in Punjab that lasted over a decade.

Anti-corruption probe in [[Brazil]], begun in March 2014 as a money-laundering inquiry into a car wash in [[Brasília|Brasília]]. It uncovered bribery in state-owned enterprises, notably the oil company Petrobras, where contractors formed a cartel. Bribes were channeled to political parties. Companies and individuals agreed to pay 25 billion reais in fines and restitution. In January 2019, Judge Sergio Moro announced he would become Justice Minister under President [[Jair Bolsonaro]], a move that drew criticism. A leak of investigators' [[Telegram (software)|Telegram]] messages damaged the probe's reputation. Moro and prosecutor Deltan Dallagnol deny wrongdoing. The task force was disbanded in February 2021.

Campaign of political repression by right-wing dictatorships of the [[Southern Cone]] of South America, combining intelligence operations, coups, and assassinations of left-wing sympathizers. It formally existed from 1975 to 1983. It was created in November 1975, when [[Augusto Pinochet]]'s spy chief, Manuel Contreras, invited 50 intelligence officers to Santiago, Chile. Initial members were Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Paraguay, and Uruguay. [[Brazil]] joined later, and [[Ecuador]] and [[Peru]] took peripheral roles. The [[United States]] backed the operation and financed its covert activities. The death toll is highly disputed; some estimates attribute at least 60,000 deaths to Condor, up to 9,000 of them in Argentina. The Argentine junta fell in 1983, weakened by its loss in the [[Falklands War]], and the fall is regarded as the end of the operation.

Allied airborne and land operation in the German-occupied Netherlands, fought September 17–25, 1944, during [[World War II]]. It aimed to create a salient 62 miles (100 km) deep into German territory, with a bridgehead over the Lower Rhine. Airborne forces seized nine bridges, and British land forces were to follow along a single road. The operation captured Eindhoven and Nijmegen but failed to secure the Rhine bridge at Arnhem. The British 1st Airborne Division suffered 8,000 dead, missing, and captured out of 10,000 men. Historian Antony Beevor called it "a bad plan right from the start."

Secret United States intelligence program that brought more than 1,600 German scientists, engineers, and technicians from [[Nazi Germany]] to the United States between 1945 and 1959. Several were confirmed to be former members of the [[Nazi Party]]. Recruits included [[Wernher von Braun]], whose team, after its 1960 transfer to [[NASA]], worked on the Saturn launch vehicles used in the [[Apollo program]]. Many had links to the Nazi rocket program, aviation, or chemical and biological warfare. The program has been valued at $10 billion USD in patents and industrial processes. Its legacy remains controversial because of recruits' Nazi affiliations.

Allied invasion of French North Africa, November 8–16, 1942, during [[World War II]]. Commanded by [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]], it was a three-pronged attack on [[Casablanca]], [[Oran]], and [[Algiers]], followed by a move on [[Tunis]] in conjunction with a British advance from Egypt. The operation was a compromise that let American forces begin fighting [[Nazi Germany]] on a limited scale. Casablanca was captured after a short siege, and Oran surrendered after bombardment by British battleships. Admiral François Darlan, commander of the Vichy French forces in Algiers, ordered cooperation with the Allies in return for becoming High Commissioner. Darlan was assassinated six weeks later.

Branch of [[Applied mathematics|applied mathematics]] that develops analytical methods to improve management and decision-making, sometimes called management science. Using techniques such as modeling, statistics, and optimization, it seeks optimal or near-optimal solutions, often maximizing profit or yield or minimizing loss, risk, or cost. It originated in military efforts before [[World War II]] and now serves industries ranging from airlines to finance and logistics. In the 17th century, [[Blaise Pascal]] and [[Christiaan Huygens]] used game-theoretic ideas and [[Expected value|expected values]] to solve decision problems, while [[Charles Babbage]]'s study of mail costs led to England's universal Penny Post in 1840. Major subdisciplines include [[Linear programming]], [[Game theory]], simulation, and queueing theory.

Order of [[Actinopterygii|ray-finned fish]] that includes the cusk-eels (family Ophidiidae), pearlfishes (family Carapidae), viviparous brotulas (family Bythitidae), and others. Members have small heads, long slender bodies, long dorsal fins, and smooth scales or none. Most come from the tropics and subtropics and live in freshwater and marine habitats, including abyssal depths. Feeding methods vary widely and include [[Parasitism|parasitism]]. Most species lay eggs, but some are viviparous. The deepest known member, *Abyssobrotula galatheae*, was found at 8,370 m (27,460 ft) in the Puerto Rico Trench. The earliest fossils, from the Maastrichtian, include *Pastorius* from [[Italy]]. Some species range as far south as the [[Weddell Sea]].

Large constellation straddling the celestial equator, with most of its area in the Southern Hemisphere. Its name comes from [[Ancient Greek]], meaning "serpent-bearer," and it is commonly represented as a man grasping a snake. [[Ptolemy]], the 2nd-century astronomer, listed it among 48 constellations, and it remains one of the 88 modern constellations. Its brightest star, Rasalhague, lies near the northern edge. It lies between [[Scorpius]] and [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]], northwest of the center of the [[Milky Way]]. In the Northern Hemisphere it is best visible in summer, and it is opposite [[Orion (constellation)|Orion]] in the sky.

Branch of [[Medicine|medicine]] concerned with the diagnosis, treatment, and surgery of eye diseases and disorders. An ophthalmologist is a physician with an MD or DO degree who completes specialty training, including a four-year residency in the United States, and may then pursue fellowship training in a subspecialty. Ophthalmologists prescribe medications, perform laser therapy and surgery, and also diagnose systemic diseases through changes seen in the eyes. Common conditions include [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]], cataracts, diabetic retinopathy, macular degeneration, and [[Refractive error|refractive errors]]. Diagnosis includes visual acuity assessment, measurement of intraocular pressure, and [[Medical imaging|imaging]] such as optical coherence tomography. The specialty has long been at the forefront of medical research.

Order of [[Arachnid|arachnids]] commonly called harvestmen or daddy longlegs, with over 6,650 species discovered worldwide. Many have exceptionally long legs, and the connection between the cephalothorax and abdomen is broad, so the body appears to be a single oval. Unlike [[Spider|spiders]], harvestmen have no venom glands or silk glands and do not build webs. Representatives of each suborder are found on all continents except [[Antarctica]]. Well-preserved fossils from the 400-million-year-old Rhynie cherts of [[Scotland]] look surprisingly modern, indicating that the basic body shape developed early.

Judgment, viewpoint, or statement that is not conclusive, as opposed to [[Fact|facts]], which are verifiable true statements. Facts can be agreed on by a consensus of experts, whereas an opinion may concern subjective matters. An opinion supported by facts and principles becomes an [[Argument|argument]]. For example, that the United States was involved in the [[Vietnam War]] is a fact, while that it was right to get involved is an opinion. People can reach opposing conclusions from the same facts, and opinions rarely change without new arguments. Public opinion, the aggregate of individual attitudes in a population, is usually estimated through [[Sampling (statistics)|survey sampling]]. In [[Political science|political science]] and [[Psychology|psychology]], group opinion concerns the views of members of a [[Jury|jury]], a legislature, or another decision-making body, including conformity and group polarization. Scientific opinion may be partial, uncertain, or conflicting, and is distinct from scientific consensus.

Survey of public opinion drawn from a sample, designed to represent a population by asking questions and extrapolating within [[Confidence interval|confidence intervals]]. The first known example was a tally of voter preferences in the 1824 presidential race, which showed [[Andrew Jackson]] leading [[John Quincy Adams]] by 335 votes to 169. In 1936 the Literary Digest's survey of 2.3 million voters suggested that Alf Landon would win, but [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] was re-elected in a landslide. Smaller, scientifically based surveys by George Gallup, Archibald Crossley, and Elmo Roper correctly predicted the result. A Gallup subsidiary in the [[United Kingdom]] was almost alone in correctly predicting Labour's victory in the 1945 general election. By the 1950s, polling had spread to most democracies.

Class of drugs that derive from, or mimic, natural substances in the [[Opium|opium]] poppy. They bind to opioid receptors in the brain and other organs, producing [[Morphine|morphine]]-like effects. Medical uses include pain relief, [[Anesthesia|anesthesia]], suppression of diarrhea, and cough suppression. The antagonist [[Naloxone|naloxone]] reverses overdose. Long-term use can cause tolerance and physical dependence, and side effects include sedation, nausea, and respiratory depression. Because opioids are addictive and can be fatal, most are controlled substances. In 2013, between 28 and 38 million people used opioids illicitly. By 2021 that number rose to 60 million.

Dried latex obtained from the seed capsules of the opium poppy (*Papaver somniferum*), containing narcotic compounds. Approximately 12 percent of opium is [[Morphine|morphine]], an alkaloid that is processed into [[Heroin|heroin]] and other synthetic opioids for medicinal use and the illegal drug trade. The latex also contains codeine and thebaine, along with non-analgesic alkaloids such as papaverine and noscapine. Traditionally, the latex is harvested by scoring the immature seed pods by hand. The Mediterranean region holds the earliest evidence of its use, dating to before 5000 BCE, with cultivation beginning around 3400 BCE in [[Mesopotamia]]. Opium was widely used for food, medicine, ritual, and as a painkiller. Modern production involves large-scale cultivation, especially in [[Afghanistan]], where recent [[Taliban|Taliban]]-led reductions cut cultivation by over 95%. Extracting morphine for the illegal drug trade reduces the bulk weight by 88%.

Marsupial mammals of the order Didelphimorphia, endemic to the Americas. With 126 species in 18 genera, it is the largest marsupial order in the Western Hemisphere. Opossums originated in South America and entered North America in the Great American Interchange after the connection of the two continents in the late [[Cenozoic]]. The oldest fossils date to the early [[Miocene]], roughly 20 million years ago. The name comes from the Powhatan language, first recorded at [[Jamestown]], Virginia, between 1607 and 1611. The [[Virginia opossum]] is the only species found in the [[United States]] and [[Canada]]. Opossums are typically nonaggressive and do not often transmit [[Rabies|rabies]].

American media mogul, actress, executive producer, author, and television personality. She is best known for *The Oprah Winfrey Show*, broadcast from [[Chicago]] in national syndication from 1986 to 2011. Born into poverty in rural [[Mississippi]] and raised partly in [[Milwaukee]], she was a local news co-anchor by age 19. She popularized a more intimate, confessional form of talk show. By the mid-1990s the show focused on literature, self-improvement, mindfulness, and spirituality. Her 2008 endorsement of [[Barack Obama]] was estimated to have been worth about one million votes in the 2008 Democratic primaries. She also formed the Oprah Winfrey Network that year. In 2013 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama. Her awards include 19 Daytime Emmy Awards and two competitive [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations.

Flat, usually disc-shaped object that stores information as physical variations on its surface, read with a beam of [[Laser|laser]] light. Discs may be reflective, with the light source and detector on the same side, or transmissive, with light passing through to the other side. Their main uses are distributing electronic media and data, and archival storage. The encoding material sits atop a thicker [[Polycarbonate|polycarbonate]] substrate, with data arranged in a continuous spiral track. Most discs show iridescence from the [[Diffraction grating|diffraction grating]] formed by their grooves. Discs have been offered in diameters between 7.6 and 30 cm, with 12 cm dominant since 1997. Discs are read-only, recordable, or rewritable. Rewritable discs typically use a phase-change alloy of silver, indium, antimony, and tellurium. Most discs lack a protective casing and are susceptible to scratches and fingerprints, although [[Blu-ray|Blu-ray discs]] have a coating called durabis.

Flexible glass or plastic fiber that transmits light from one end to the other, widely used in [[Telecommunications|fiber-optic communication]]. Fibers carry signals over longer distances and at higher bandwidths than electrical [[Electrical cable|cables]], with less loss and immunity to electromagnetic interference. Light is kept in a core surrounded by cladding of lower [[Refractive index|refractive index]], through total internal reflection. Single-mode fibers carry most links longer than 1,050 meters (3,440 ft), while multi-mode fibers suit short links and high-power transmission. Glass fibers are typically made by drawing, and fibers are also used for illumination, imaging, and [[Sensor|sensors]]. Light was first guided by refraction in [[Paris]] in the early 1840s, and John Tyndall demonstrated it in [[London]] about 12 years later.

Visually perceived image that arguably differs from reality, caused by the [[Visual system|visual system]]. Richard Gregory classified illusions as physical, physiological, or cognitive, with four kinds in each class: ambiguities, distortions, paradoxes, and fictions. A classic physical distortion is the apparent bending of a stick half immersed in water, discussed by [[Ptolemy]] (c. 150). An afterimage is a physiological fiction. Cognitive illusions, such as the Ponzo, Poggendorff, and Müller-Lyer illusions, arise from unconscious inferences, an idea first suggested by Hermann Helmholtz in the 19th century. Pathological illusions arise from changes in perceptual mechanisms and are discussed under [[Hallucination|visual hallucinations]]. Illusions can also aid the monitoring and rehabilitation of disorders such as [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]] and phantom limb syndrome.

Instrument that uses visible light and a system of [[Lens|lenses]] to produce magnified images of small objects, also called a light microscope. Microscopes of this kind are the oldest type, and the compound form appeared in the 17th century. [[Galileo Galilei]] developed an improved compound microscope in 1609. In a compound microscope, an objective lens forms a real image that an eyepiece magnifies, and most modern research microscopes are of this type. Specimens may be lit from below, or by light passing through (bright field) or around (dark field) the objective. Phase-contrast imaging increases contrast by highlighting small details of differing refractive index. Resolving power is typically limited to around 200 nanometers by the [[Diffraction|diffraction]] limit of visible light, so larger magnification reveals no more detail. Alternatives such as electron microscopes, which do not use visible light, can achieve much greater magnifications.
